title: Easy Come, Easy Go? Examining the Perceptions and Learning Effects of LLM-based Chatbot in the Context of Search-as-Learning
extended_summary:
This paper investigates whether LLM-based chatbots help or hinder learning in Search-as-Learning (SAL), a process in which learners acquire knowledge by seeking and organizing information. The authors focus on a central tension: chatbots make information access faster and more answer-centric, but this may reduce cognitive effort and lead to shallower learning. The study asks both how students and educators perceive these trade-offs and how chatbot-supported learning actually compares with textbook-based and search-engine-based SAL in terms of efficiency, immediate learning, and delayed retention.

The intervention compares three SAL modalities: textbooks, Google search, and ChatGPT-4o. The researchers first conducted surveys with 75 educators and 92 university students to gather perceived benefits, risks, and preferences. They then ran a controlled within-subjects experiment with the 92 students, who completed SAL tasks in all three conditions in randomized counterbalanced order across three consecutive days. In each condition, students studied STEM topics using a custom browser-based SAL Logger, generated their own search questions, took notes, reviewed their notes, drew concept maps, and completed closed-book multiple-choice tests. A delayed retention test using the same questions was administered two weeks later.

The population was primarily South Korean university students and educators, with the student experiment conducted at the authors’ institute in South Korea in a university-level STEM context. Educators were mostly based in South Korea, though two were based in the United States. The student sample consisted of 92 undergraduates, and the educator sample included teachers working in educational institutes, mainly university and high school teachers. The study context was a web-based experimental learning environment rather than normal classroom instruction.

The main conclusion is that LLM-based chatbots improve short-term learning efficiency and immediate conceptual understanding relative to books, and perform similarly to search engines on many measures, but they do not produce superior long-term retention. Chatbot use led to more search Q&A cycles, less time per cycle, richer concept maps, and higher immediate test scores than books, especially at Bloom’s Understand level. However, after two weeks, retention did not differ significantly among chatbot, search engine, and book conditions. Survey findings showed that students preferred chatbots for speed and selectivity, while educators worried about reduced metacognition and cognitive engagement. Overall, the paper concludes that chatbots support efficient short-term learning without causing the long-term deficit educators feared, but they also do not enhance deeper or more durable learning on their own.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's conversational large language model chatbot used for interactive question answering and synthesized explanations.
identified_tools.use_case: Used as the chatbot condition in a within-subject Search-as-Learning experiment, where university students used ChatGPT-4o without web browsing to study STEM topics and were compared against books and Google search.

findings.finding_summary: In the 40-minute Search-as-Learning task, students completed more search Q&A pairs with ChatGPT than with books: 614 total Q&A pairs in the Chatbot condition versus 442 in the Book condition; per student, M=6.69 (SD=5.47) for Chatbot versus M=4.59 (SD=2.91) for Book, with Chatbot > Book (p<.002). Students also spent less time per Q&A pair in the Chatbot condition (M=4.77 minutes, SD=4.97) than in the Book condition (M=6.87, SD=6.57; p<.001) and Search Engine condition (M=5.95, SD=5.58; p=.05).
findings.measure: Number of search Q&A pairs completed; average time spent per Q&A pair

findings.finding_summary: Concept-map outputs indicated higher immediate information throughput for ChatGPT than books. The Chatbot condition produced more nodes (M=23.76, SD=10.00) than the Book condition (M=18.67, SD=7.71), F(2,272)=7.20, p<.001, and more edges (M=32.83, SD=17.45) than the Book condition (M=25.67, SD=15.42), F(2,272)=4.13, p<.05.
findings.measure: Closed-book concept map structure: number of nodes and number of edges

findings.finding_summary: On the immediate closed-book test (0-9 scale), ChatGPT produced the highest scores (M=5.80, SD=1.55), outperforming the Book condition (M=4.83, SD=1.67), with Chatbot > Book (p<.001); overall ANOVA was F(2,272)=9.59, p<.001. By Bloom level, the advantage was confined to the Understand level: Chatbot M=2.07 (SD=0.80) versus Book M=1.58 (SD=0.85), p<.001, with no significant differences at Apply or Analyze levels.
findings.measure: Immediate closed-book MCQ test scores overall and by Bloom's taxonomy level

findings.finding_summary: On the two-week delayed retention test, ChatGPT did not differ significantly from books or search engines after adjusting for immediate test performance. Adjusted retention means were Chatbot M=5.05, Search Engine M=5.15, and Book M=5.16; the closed-book test score significantly predicted retention, F(1,272)=96.78, p<.001, but there were no significant between-condition differences, including at the Understand, Apply, and Analyze levels.
findings.measure: Two-week delayed retention MCQ test scores, overall and by Bloom's taxonomy level, analyzed via ANCOVA with closed-book score as covariate
findings.effect_size: F(1,272)=96.78 for covariate; between-condition effect not significant

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: Generic LLM-based chatbots used for conversational information seeking, synthesized explanations, and dialogue-based learning support.
identified_tools.use_case: Studied in educator and student surveys as a general category of LLM-based chatbots for Search-as-Learning, focusing on perceived benefits, risks, and tool preferences.

findings.finding_summary: Survey findings showed a divergence in preferences: educators strongly preferred conventional tools over LLM-based chatbots, while students showed the opposite pattern. Among educators (N=75), 52% preferred books, 36% search engines, and 12% LLM-based chatbots; a Friedman test found significant differences in rankings across tools, X^2(2)=21.62, p<.001, and students' preference for LLM-based chatbots over books was statistically significant (p<.001).
findings.measure: Ranked preferences for SAL tools from educator and student surveys

findings.finding_summary: Both educators and students recognized benefits of LLM-based chatbots for Search-as-Learning, especially time efficiency, diverse explanations, and personalized learning, but also noted risks. Educators most frequently cited time efficiency (50 mentions), limited cognitive engagement (37), personalized learning (26), reduced metacognition (23), and lack of reliability (19), while students most frequently cited lack of reliability (39), time efficiency (36), diverse explanations (29), prior knowledge dependency (24), and selective learning (14).
findings.measure: Qualitative survey themes on perceived benefits and risks

quality_tier_rationale: The paper includes a controlled within-subject empirical experiment with n=92 and clear comparative outcome measures, but it is not a randomized controlled trial in the K-12 intervention sense and also includes perception surveys, so there are some causal and generalizability concerns.
impact_tier_rationale: ChatGPT showed clear short-term advantages on efficiency and immediate understanding outcomes, but no durable advantage on delayed retention and no reported standardized effect sizes. Overall impact is positive but limited and unclear in magnitude over time.
